questions.question_text: Find the equation of the line with gradient $8$ and $y$-intercept $(0, 5)$.

options.why: Used point-gradient form $y - 5 = 8x$ but left the $-5$ on the right-hand side instead of adding $5$ to both sides.
Swapped the gradient and the $y$-intercept, putting $5$ in the $m$ position and $8$ in the $c$ position.
Swapped the gradient and the $y$-intercept and then left the constant on the right-hand side as $-8$ instead of $+8$.

options.why: Made the constant positive when the intercept is $-3$.
Used the intercept as the gradient and the gradient as the intercept.
Swapped the two values, keeping the negative on the wrong one.

Write its equation.

questions.question_text: Find the equation of the line with gradient $-7$ and $y$-intercept $(0, 0)$.

options.why: Dropped the negative sign on the gradient.
Left off the $x$; a gradient multiplies $x$.
Inverted the gradient instead of using it directly.

questions.solution_text:
$m = -7$ and $c = 0$, so the constant drops out.
$y = -7x$

questions.question_text: Find the equation of the line with gradient $1$ and $y$-intercept $(0, 6)$.

options.why: Used the $y$-intercept as the gradient and the gradient as the intercept.
Made the $y$-intercept negative when it is $+6$.
Changed the sign of the gradient, which is $+1$.

questions.solution_text:
$m = 1$ and $c = 6$. A gradient of $1$ is written without a number.
$y = x + 6$

questions.question_text: Find the equation of the line with gradient $-\frac{3}{4}$ and $y$-intercept $(0, 0)$.

options.why: Dropped the negative sign on the gradient.
Inverted the fractional gradient.
Left off the $x$; a gradient multiplies $x$.

questions.solution_text:
$m = -\frac{3}{4}$ and $c = 0$, so the constant drops out.
$y = -\frac{3}{4}x$

questions.question_text:
The $y$-intercept and the gradient step of a line are shown.
Write the equation of the line.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=6cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-5,xmax=5,ymin=-6,ymax=6,xtick={-4,-2,2,4},ytick={-4,-2,2,4,6},minor x tick num=1,minor y tick num=1,grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=1.8pt] coordinates {(0,3) (1,1)};\draw[dashed,gray] (axis cs:0,3)--(axis cs:1,3)--(axis cs:1,1);\node[below,font=\small] at (axis cs:0.5,3){$1$};\node[right,font=\small] at (axis cs:1,2){$2$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Read the downward step as a positive gradient.
Made the $y$-intercept negative when the line crosses at $+3$.
Used run over rise instead of rise over run for the gradient.

questions.solution_text:
The $y$-intercept is $(0, 3)$, so $c = 3$.
The step is right $1$ and down $2$, so the gradient is $\frac{-2}{1} = -2$.
$y = -2x + 3$
